title: Both moral realism and relativism are wrong
subtitle: Stripping morality of metaphysics
author: Melis Erdur
introduction: In what sense is morality objective? Moral realists argue that there are moral facts whose truth is independent of what anyone thinks, while moral relativists argue that moral claims are only true relative to a particular culture or society. In this article, Melis Erdur argues that both moral realism and moral relativism are self-defeating. She argues that we should dispense with overarching metaphysical stories of where morality comes from – moral shortcuts – and instead learn to stand firm in our own human convictions.
body:
‘Are there objective moral truths?’ This question may sound academic and technical, calling for expertise in “moral metaphysics”. But just like any other significant question concerning morality, it boils down to an ordinary moral question that each one of us can and must answer. The question in the case of the “objectivity of morality” is, ‘Should we have a moral backbone, standing firm in our strongest moral convictions?’ And both moral realists and moral relativists are giving the wrong answer. Let me explain.

Moral realism is the view that there are objective moral truths – that is, moral truths that are independent of what anyone thinks. Realists argue by appeal to cases such as slavery, genocide, and their somewhat disturbing favorite, “torturing babies for fun”, which they hope to be uncontroversially immoral. They ask, ‘Aren’t these things wrong? And wouldn’t they be wrong even if “society” thought they were great? When (for thousands of years) most people thought that slavery was an acceptable fact of life, wasn’t slavery still wrong?’ And they answer, ‘Of course. Therefore, you must agree that some things are wrong independently of what anyone thinks.’

Moral relativism, on the other hand, is the view that moral truths are always relative to societies or cultures. Relativists typically argue by appeal to cases from history in which some people thought that they had “the objective moral truth” on their side when they engaged in evil practices like racism and slavery. Relativists say, ‘Look at all those cases in which moral hubris accompanied dehumanization and violence. If we want to avoid such evil things, we must regard our moral convictions as just what we think. We shouldn’t assume that they apply to everyone.’

If you genuinely care about racism and slavery, you can’t also think that this is just what you think. You must stand firm in your anti-racism and anti-slavery.

Now, notice that under the guise of having a metaphysical debate about “the nature of moral truths”, the two sides are having an unmistakably moral argument. The moral realist is claiming that slavery, genocide, and torturing babies for fun are so obviously wrong that we ought to be confident in our moral convictions and judge such things to be wrong even for cultures that think differently. The moral relativist is claiming that we ought never to be confident in our moral convictions because such confidence sometimes leads to evils like racism and slavery. Neither side has any “metaphysical” evidence for anything – they are just telling us what strikes them as wrong and what we should do about it. Stripped of all the philosophical noise, the issue comes down to this: Should we stand firm in our strongest moral convictions?

The moral relativist is essentially saying that we shouldn’t stand firm even in our strongest moral convictions because that sometimes leads to evils like racism and slavery. But this is an unstable, self-undermining position. It requires our firm moral conviction that racism and slavery are wrong to argue that we should never stand firm in our moral convictions. For, if you are to doubt all your moral convictions, why don’t you also doubt that racism and slavery are wrong? It is just what you think, after all. But if you can’t even be confident that racism and slavery are wrong, what reason do you have to be a moral relativist in the first place?

Moral relativism is in essence the view that it is always morally wrong to take your moral judgment seriously. But that is plain nonsense. And its only effect is to paralyze decent people – who are outraged by things like racism and slavery – with self-doubt. If you genuinely care about racism and slavery, you can’t also think that this is just what you think. You must stand firm in your anti-racism and anti-slavery.

SUGGESTED READING Moving past morality By Joel Marks

Now let’s turn to the moral realist. Since he denies that right and wrong are relative to societies, it may appear that the realist is standing on morally firm footing. But a closer examination reveals that that is not at all the case. The moral realist claims that whether racism, slavery, and genocide are wrong is determined by an independent moral reality that has nothing to do with what anyone thinks. But here is the question: what if it turns out that this so-called moral reality dictates that slavery, racism, and genocide are morally right? Would they then be right?

Realists commonly respond by claiming that moral reality cannot turn out to be like that – that it cannot, for instance, dictate that our true moral obligation is to commit genocide and practice slavery. They engage in all sorts of philosophical gymnastics to assure us that such moral misfortune cannot befall us. But their optimism is baseless. We have no reason to think that an independent moral reality, which has nothing to do with what we consider good and decent, will miraculously turn out to align perfectly with our fundamental values. Therefore, a consistent moral realist must grant that our true moral obligation may turn out to be committing genocide and practicing slavery – in which case, according to the realist, that is what we ought to do. That is not exactly standing morally firm!

We have to do the moral work every time. There are no moral shortcuts.

Then how do we do it?  How do we stand firm in our strongest moral convictions? The best we can do is focus on the proper moral work and not undermine that work with misguided philosophical accounts of morality. The proper moral work involves diligently investigating the facts pertaining to each case, thinking hard and seriously, and being consistent and open to criticism. Once we do the moral work and conclude that racism or oppression of women is clearly wrong, say, we must stand firm in that judgment. Not because it is our judgment but because it is a well-considered judgment. We must challenge and fight against racism and oppression of women wherever we encounter them, and not tolerate or respect them because they belong to someone’s “culture”.

If we are confronted with counterclaims or counterarguments, we must do the moral work again. That is what it takes to be moral. We have to do the moral work every time. There are no moral shortcuts. That is why all philosophical accounts proposing one thing or the other as the ultimate moral source or authority are misguided. They are all looking for someone or something that could, in theory, just give us all the right answers to moral questions. But there is no such thing. Because it is always morally wrong to uncritically adopt a moral view, without doing the necessary moral work – even if it is sent from “morality”. When it comes to morality, we always have to think for ourselves.  Otherwise, it is slavery, and you know what we think about that…
